lesson.text: You have used every one of these. Now learn their names.

PRIVACY ENHANCING TECHNOLOGIES (PETs) are the tools that reduce privacy risk while keeping data useful. You have reached for most of them already, village-disguised. This module is the cabinet where they all hang, labelled at last. They sit on a spectrum — from simply hiding WHO, to letting others compute on data they can never actually read.

PETS YOU HAVE ALREADY USED

PSEUDONYMISATION — replace identifiers with codes (Agent NIGHTINGALE; Ticket T-822). Reversible wherever a key exists, and still personal data under the law. Lowers exposure, not risk entirely.

GENERALISATION & SUPPRESSION — blur specifics into ranges, star out the rest, until each record hides in a crowd (the Archive's Safehouse Log audit). The k=2 promise you tested — and broke, at S-08.

AGGREGATION — report the statistics, drop the individuals (Maren's Statistician's Desk: raw logs in, illness counts out). Strong when the purpose only needs the distribution.

ENCRYPTION — lock the contents so only a key-holder reads them, in transit (the Cipher Desk on the Post Road) and at rest (the Iron Vault). Protects confidentiality without changing the data itself.

ACCESS CONTROL & MINIMISATION — give each party only the field it needs (the sorting desk got the address, never the contents). Not a single gadget but the discipline the others serve.

PETS NOT YET ISSUED (HIGHER CLEARANCE)

DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY — add carefully calibrated NOISE to results so the answer about the GROUP stays accurate while no single person can be picked out, even by someone who already knows everything else about everyone. The mathematical successor to k-anonymity's 'hide in the crowd.'

SECURE COMPUTATION / HOMOMORPHIC ENCRYPTION — the alchemist's dream: compute on data that stays encrypted the entire time, so a party can produce an answer without ever seeing the inputs. Two guilds could learn a shared total without either revealing its own books. (These await you — the cabinet's locked drawer.)

The lesson is not to memorise the cabinet but to CHOOSE from it. PETs are not interchangeable. Each defends a different point in the data's life, and each trades away something — usually UTILITY for PROTECTION. Encryption guards data you must still store whole; aggregation destroys detail you no longer need; differential privacy protects individuals inside a published statistic; pseudonymisation buys you a little distance, not anonymity. The skill is matching the tool to the purpose and the risk — enough protection to serve the duty, enough utility to serve the purpose.

THE TEST YOU'LL ACTUALLY FACE — Given a situation, which PET? Ask: what does the recipient truly NEED (a statistic? a single record? just a yes/no?), and what is the WORST that leaks if this is breached? The gap between those two answers is the PET-shaped hole to fill.
Choose well and you achieve what the law calls data protection BY DESIGN: the risk removed at the source, so the systems downstream never hold the danger in the first place.

quiz.q: The Council needs only to know HOW MANY villagers had each illness this winter — never who. Which PET fits best?
explain: Encryption keeps the individual records unreadable to outsiders, but the records — and the people inside them — are still stored whole. The Council doesn't need to store people at all here.
Correct — the purpose only needs the distribution, not the people. Count and drop identifiers at the source, the way Maren's desk turns raw logs straight into illness counts.
A pseudonym still describes one person, just under a different name. It hides WHO, not the fact that an individual record exists at all — more than this purpose needs.

quiz.q: A guest ledger is 'anonymised' by turning ages into ranges and starring out towns — yet one row is still unique. This PET, and its failure mode?
choices: Generalisation/suppression — fails if any record stays unique
Encryption — fails if the key leaks
Aggregation — fails if numbers are small
explain: Correct — this is k-anonymity built from generalisation (ranges) and suppression (stars). Every record must hide in a crowd of at least k; a single unique combination breaks the promise for that one person, no matter how well the rest of the ledger is blurred.
No key was ever involved — ranges and stars aren't ciphertext, they're the data itself, permanently blurred. A leaked key isn't the failure mode here.
Aggregation would have reported totals and dropped the rows entirely — this ledger still has individual rows, just blurred ones. Its failure is a unique row, not a small count.

quiz.q: Sensitive records must be STORED WHOLE for treatment, but must be unreadable if the vault is stolen. Which PET?
explain: Aggregation would destroy exactly the detail treatment needs — you can't dose a patient from a headcount.
Correct — you can't aggregate or noise data you still need to read back in full later. Lock it instead, so a thief who steals the vault gets ciphertext, not records. The Iron Vault.
Differential privacy protects a published STATISTIC about a group — it has nothing to say about a single patient's full record sitting in storage.

quiz.q: You must PUBLISH useful statistics about villagers, and assume an attacker who already knows everything about everyone EXCEPT their target. Which PET is built for exactly this adversary?
explain: A pseudonym does nothing for a PUBLISHED statistic — there's no code to reverse in an aggregate number, and this attacker isn't trying to un-mask a record anyway.

Correct — calibrated noise makes any single person's presence undetectable in the published result, even against an attacker who knows everything else. The guarantee k-anonymity can't make once an attacker has outside knowledge.
Access control governs who may reach the data before it's published — once the statistic is public, there's nothing left to control access to.

quiz.q: Two guilds want to learn their COMBINED total sales without either revealing its own books to the other. Which PET makes this possible?
choices: Give both books to a trusted third party
explain: Correct — compute on data that stays encrypted the entire time, so the shared total comes out while each guild's own books stay secret. No trusted third party required. The cabinet's locked drawer.
Pseudonymising the books still leaves the numbers themselves fully readable — a coded name on a ledger does nothing to hide the sales figures within it.
This works, but it's the thing PETs let you avoid — now a third party holds both books whole, and the guilds' secrecy depends entirely on trusting them not to look, or not to be robbed.
